children: New Delhi, Nov. 8 -- Today, as everyone celebrates Diwali across the nation, it is a festival that often offers an opportunity to exchange gifts, cash, vouchers, and other valuable items as tokens of appreciation and affection for near and dear ones. Still, receiving expensive gifts from friends, family, or employers may have different income tax implications.

That is why, if you are someone who is planning to gift your near and dear ones or friends, or if your employer has gifted you with valuables, it becomes indispensable for you to clearly understand the tax implications of the gifts, because having clarity on this can help you plan your finances better and ensure that the celebrations of the festival of light brighten up the lives of your friends and family.

Now, gifts from certain 'relatives' are exempt without any monetary limit, whereas gifts from non-relatives are subject to a Rs.50,000 threshold. This write-up focuses on the possible tax implications in different cases.

Hence, the question arises: if you receive Diwali gifts worth Rs.50,000 or more from friends, will you have to pay tax on the entire amount or only the excess? The answer to this question is not straightforward; it depends entirely on the aggregate value of gifts received during the financial year and the relationship between the gift provider and the eventual recipient.
Swati Jain, CA, CEO, Wealth, Arihant Capital Markets, explains the tax treatment across three different situations.

As per the income tax rules, gifts received from friends are taxable if their aggregate value exceeds Rs.50,000 during a financial year. Furthermore, do note, the entire amount becomes taxable in such a case, not just the portion exceeding the threshold.

Jain explained this stating: "Total gifts from non-relatives up to Rs.50,000 in a financial year are tax-free. If the aggregate total crosses Rs.50,000, the entire amount is fully taxable at your income tax slab rates. Let's understand it with two scenarios. Scenario 1: You received Rs.30,000 in gifts during Diwali and had already received Rs.25,000 earlier in the financial year; your total is Rs.55,000. Because it crossed Rs.50,000, the entire Rs.55,000 is taxed at your slab rate. Scenario 2: Now, let's say you received Rs.30,000 for Diwali and Rs.15,000 earlier in the year; your total is Rs.45,000. Since this is below Rs.50,000, you pay zero tax."

Therefore, the recipients should account for all gifts from non-relatives during the year rather than considering Diwali gifts in isolation in order to ensure accurate tax compliance at the end of the financial year.

Gifts from specified relatives are completely tax-free, irrespective of their value. These include gifts from parents, siblings, spouses and children, among other relationships recognised under the law.
On this, Jain added: "Completely tax-free with no monetary limit, as long as the giver falls under the official definition of a 'relative' (such as parents, siblings, spouse, or children)."

Employer gifts are treated differently. Jain explained the tax treatment of such gifts, stating: "If your employer gifts cash or cash equivalents, then it will be fully taxable as salary. However, gifts in kind/vouchers are tax-free up to Rs.15,000 per financial year."

Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, non-cash gifts, vouchers and tokens are exempt only when their aggregate value is below Rs.15,000 during the tax year. At Rs.15,000 or above, the entire value becomes taxable as a salary perquisite.

In summary, the tax treatment of Diwali gifts depends on factors such as who gives them, their aggregate value, when they are given, i.e., whether in the same financial year or not, and the applicable exemption.

Recipients should maintain proper records of valuable gifts and seek professional advice when filing their income tax returns to ensure accurate and timely compliance with tax authorities. Keeping these core basics in mind, gifts can also be planned this Diwali and for months ahead.
